summary: Defines how to convert contact information between JSContact and vCard. It gives conversion rules for every JSContact and vCard element registered with IANA at publication time, and defines new properties and parameters so unknown or custom elements can still be converted. It updates RFC 6350.

plainLanguage.summary: JSContact stores contact cards as JSON, and vCard stores them as text lines. This RFC says exactly how to turn one into the other, property by property, and gives both formats a place to put anything that has no standard name yet.

questions: how to convert vcard to jscontact
subtitle: Rules for converting contact cards between the JSContact (JSON) and vCard formats, including data neither side has a place for.

tldr.problem: JSContact is meant as an alternative to vCard and jCard, but applications that prefer JSContact still have to talk to services and clients that only understand vCard or jCard, and the same is true in the other direction.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives conversion rules for every JSContact and vCard element registered with IANA at the time of publication. For anything with no registered counterpart, it defines the JSContact properties vCardProps, vCardParams and vCardName, the vCard property JSPROP and the vCard parameters JSCOMPS and JSPTR.
tldr.outcome: A card can be converted in either direction, and unknown or custom elements can survive the round trip. The RFC updates RFC 6350 and is itself updated by RFC 9982.

today: RFC 9555 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2024. It updates RFC 6350 and is itself updated by RFC 9982. The conversion rules themselves are in RFC 9553 and RFC 9554.

sections.title: Why a Conversion Specification Is Needed
sections.content:
The JSContact data model and format, defined in RFC 9553, is meant as an alternative to the widely used vCard format of RFC 6350 and to the jCard format of RFC 7095.

Applications may prefer JSContact for exchanging contact card data, but they are likely to have to interoperate with services and clients that only support vCard or jCard. Providers and consumers that already use vCard or jCard may also want to represent the same data in JSContact. This document therefore defines standard rules for converting contact data between JSContact and vCard, and so between JSContact and jCard.

The rules follow the structure of vCard version 4, and the properties and parameters of vCard extension RFCs, including those in RFC 9554, are added to the appropriate subsections. The abstract syntax used throughout is the ABNF of RFC 5234 and of RFC 6350.
sections.plainLanguage: Many systems only read one of the two formats, so a card has to be able to move between them without losing anything. This RFC is the rulebook for that move.

sections.title: General Rules: The uid and the Identifiers
sections.content:
The UID property is optional in vCard but the Card object's uid property is mandatory in JSContact. An implementation that converts a vCard without a UID property must generate a unique identifier for the uid property. That value should be the same every time the same vCard is converted, though how to achieve that is left to the implementation.

Multivalued properties in JSContact are usually represented as a JSON object whose keys are of the Id type and whose values are the converted vCard property. Without the PROP-ID parameter, an implementation may choose any identifier as the key, but the values it generates must be valid Id values, for example a counter that runs across all the identifier keys of a Card, or one that is unique only inside a single JSON object.
sections.plainLanguage: Every card needs a unique identifier, so a vCard without one gets one made up during the conversion. The keys that name the several values of a repeated property are also chosen by the implementation, but they must be valid identifiers.

sections.title: Value Types and Their JSContact Equivalents
sections.content:
Each vCard value type has a JSContact counterpart. BOOLEAN becomes the JSContact Boolean type. TIMESTAMP becomes a UTCDateTime, except for anniversaries, which become a Timestamp. A DATE used for an anniversary becomes a PartialDate object, unless the value holds only a month or only a day. TIME, DATE-TIME, DATE-AND-OR-TIME, and DATE values that define only a month or a day do not become a JSContact datetime type at all; the properties and parameters that carry them convert under the rules for extended content.

INTEGER becomes the Int and UnsignedInt types, and FLOAT becomes the JSContact Number type. LANGUAGE-TAG and TEXT both become the JSContact String type, as does URI, whose value must be a URI as defined in RFC 3986. A UTC-OFFSET either becomes a String holding a name from the IANA Time Zone Database, or does not convert to any JSContact type.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is mostly one to one: a date becomes a date, a number becomes a number, a piece of text becomes a string. A few vCard types, such as a time of day, have no JSContact equivalent and are handled by the rules for content that has no standard home.

sections.title: Structured Values: Names and Addresses
sections.content:
Some vCard properties hold a structured value, a semicolon-separated list of components. The ADR property converts to an Address object in the Card object's addresses property, and each component of the structured value becomes an AddressComponent. The table in the RFC maps the vCard components to the JSContact component kinds: the post office box becomes postOfficeBox, the extended address becomes apartment, the street address becomes name, the locality, region and postal code keep their names, and the components added by RFC 9554, such as building, floor, landmark, subdistrict and district, have kinds of their own. The new components should be set even when their values are empty.

The order of the components matters, and a vCard value can use separators between them. The JSCOMPS parameter, defined later in this RFC, records that order and the separator values. When it is set, the Address object's isOrdered property is "true" and the components follow the order of the parameter. When it is not set, isOrdered is "false" and the components follow the order of the values in the vCard structured value, read from left to right. The LABEL parameter becomes the Address object's full property, the GEO parameter becomes its coordinates, the TZ parameter becomes its time zone, and the CC parameter becomes its country code.
sections.plainLanguage: An address in vCard is one line with several parts separated by semicolons. In JSContact it becomes an object with a named part for each piece, and a parameter records the order the parts came in and the separators between them.

sections.title: Keeping What Has No Registered Home
sections.content:
A vCard may hold properties or parameters for which no registered JSContact property exists, for instance vendor extensions or properties whose meaning the implementation does not know. The RFC defines three JSContact properties that can carry them.

vCardProps is a list of jCard-encoded vCard properties that are set in the vCard the JSContact object represents. vCardParams holds the vCard parameters set on the property that converts to this JSContact object, as an object of parameter names to values. vCardName holds the name of the vCard element that the object came from, which is useful when two different vCard properties convert to the same JSContact type, such as IMPP and SOCIALPROFILE, which both become an OnlineService object. Implementations may convert differently if they judge that more appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: When a card holds something neither format has a name for, the JSContact side has three places to put it: the whole unknown properties, the unknown parameters of a known property, and the name of the original vCard element.

sections.title: Converting JSContact Back to vCard
sections.content:
A Card object converts to vCard by applying the reverse of the rules above, and Appendix A of the RFC lists those reverse rules. On top of them, a multivalued JSContact property becomes separate instances of its vCard equivalent, and the PROP-ID parameter of each instance must be set to the Id key of the converted value.

The full name is a special case. The full property of the name object is optional in JSContact, but the FN property is mandatory in vCard. If the full property is set, its value must be used. If it is not, the full name should be derived from the components of the name object: by concatenating them when the isOrdered property is "true", or by any other heuristic otherwise, such as the person-name rules of the Unicode Common Locale Data Repository. In that case the DERIVED parameter must be set on the FN property. If neither is available, the FN property must be set to the empty value.

For the other direction, the RFC defines the JSPROP vCard property, which holds an arbitrary JSContact property as a JSON-encoded TEXT value, and the JSPTR parameter, whose value is a JSON pointer to the property inside the Card. The root of the pointer is always the Card object, and the pointer must not point into an array. All the JSPROP properties of a vCard together form a PatchObject, and that object may only be applied once every other vCard property has been converted. The JSCOMPS parameter records the order and the separators of the elements of a structured value, and its presence is what makes the JSContact object ordered.
sections.plainLanguage: Going back to vCard, the rules run in reverse. Anything JSContact has that vCard has no name for is carried in a JSON-encoded property, and a pointer says where in the card it belongs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This specification defines how to convert between the JSContact and vCard formats, so the security considerations for parsing and formatting such data apply. They are set out in Section 4 of RFC 9553 and Section 9 of RFC 6350.

The IANA registries are updated by the RFC: a new vCard property, JSPROP, and a new vCard parameter, JSPTR, and three new JSContact properties, vCardName, vCardParams and vCardProps, together with a new JSContact type, JCardProp. All of them have a Since Version of 1.0 and are under the IETF change controller.
sections.plainLanguage: Converting a card means parsing untrusted data, so the same parsing rules that apply to the two formats apply here. The RFC also registers the new names it introduces.
